clue.text: Won invasion beach-head ? A come-down for Wellington

definitions.meaning: a beachhead taken by assault is a landing won by force against resistance
the Wellington was an RAF bomber; an emergency touchdown away from an airfield is a come-down for it

explanation.surface: A wartime tale of a captured beach and a humbling setback for the Duke of Wellington.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wellington' suggests the Iron Duke, but here it is the twin-engined Vickers Wellington bomber of the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses describe an arrival by force: troops storming ashore, or an aircraft obliged to come down unexpectedly.

clue.text: Traitor makes date with Guy, press writer

parts.note: Guy Fawkes Night falls on the fifth of November, the date tied to Guy
a columnist writes a regular column for the press

explanation.surface: A turncoat arranges to meet Guy and a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy Fawkes, the Gunpowder Plot conspirator, is remembered in Britain every 5 November with bonfires.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from the Spanish Civil War for a hidden group of sympathisers working for the enemy within, so a traitor.

clue.text: Events at 23 12s possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters may be arranged another way

parts.note: the answer to 12 across is ACRE; the plural gives ACRES

explanation.surface: Something happening across many acres at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references point to 23 across (ASCOT, the Berkshire racecourse) and 12 across (ACRE); rearrange ACRES to get the meetings held there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a racecourse, so the events held there are horse races.

clue.text: Lineage gives us a professional pull ?

definitions.meaning: lineage means descent or ancestry, as in 'of French origin'
a dentist's work in pulling out a tooth

explanation.surface: Ancestry treated as a matter of having the right connections in a profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull' looks like influence or string-pulling, but it is literal: a dentist drawing a tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both descent or ancestry and the drawing out of a tooth by a dentist.

clue.text: Man shows age with peripheral fat

indicators.note: peripheral means lying around the edge, so the fat wraps around the age

parts.note: lard is pig fat
an eon is a very long age

explanation.surface: A fellow showing his years and some flab around the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with peripheral' says the fat sits around the age: EON goes inside LARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonard is a man's first name.

clue.text: No way to drink medicine

parts.note: taken as written
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Refusing any route towards drinking one's medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack remedy or patent medicine.

clue.text: Foot upset jolly good doctor

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read bottom to top

parts.note: A1 means first-rate; written with I for the figure 1 it is AI
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor who is very cheerful is knocked over by a foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns AI to give IA; then MB follows.
explanation.definitionFit: In verse, a foot is a unit of metre, and this one is a short syllable followed by a long one.

clue.text: Drink or two holding up Reg

indicators.note: holding means the two drinks surround what comes next

parts.note: two drinks here are gin and ale, side by side

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the name is read from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written, a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone offered a drink or two keeps Reg upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns REG into GER, which goes between GIN and ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ginger-flavoured fizzy soft drink, often a mixer.

clue.text: Nearly exhausted — longest lane's so winding

indicators.note: winding suggests twisting, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: the letters of lane's, with the S kept

explanation.surface: Worn out because the longest lane winds on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange LONGEST, LANES and SO, fourteen letters, to get the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone close to collapse, as a worn-out animal barely able to stand.

clue.text: Jocose characters could be cause of it

indicators.note: the letters of the following words could be made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Joking characters might be the reason for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange the letters of CAUSE OF IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocose and facetious are synonyms, both meaning flippantly joking.

clue.text: Prévost's heroine French but not Italian

definitions.meaning: the Abbé Prévost's novel tells of the courtesan ... Lescaut
Massenet's French opera on the story uses only her first name; Puccini's Italian one adds Lescaut

explanation.surface: A literary heroine claimed by France but denied to Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Both operas tell the same story: Massenet's French version is titled with her first name alone, while Puccini's Italian version is 'Manon Lescaut'.
explanation.definitionFit: The courtesan in the 1731 novel by the Abbé Prévost is called by this first name, which is also the title of Massenet's opera.

clue.text: Water-carrier meets a prophet

parts.note: a hose carries water

explanation.surface: A water-bearer encounters a holy prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water-carrier' suggests Aquarius or a jug, but here it is a garden hose.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosea is an Old Testament prophet with a book of the Bible named after him.

clue.text: The port Macready swallowed

indicators.note: swallowed means the word holds the answer within it

explanation.surface: The actor Macready gulping down some port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: William Macready was a famous Victorian actor; 'port' looks like the wine, but it is a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Acre is an ancient harbour town in northern Israel.

clue.text: Spanish-American finds enclosure empty

indicators.note: finds is read as the pen finding something inside it

parts.note: a pen is an enclosure for animals
O, a nought, stands for empty or nothing

explanation.surface: A Latin American discovers an empty pen.
explanation.definitionFit: A peon is a landless labourer in Spanish America.

clue.text: Hope for a price of course on one share

parts.note: SP is starting price, the odds at a racecourse
I is the Roman numeral for one
a ration is a share

explanation.surface: Wishing for a good price at the racecourse on one share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' is a racecourse; SP is the starting price, a horse's betting odds when the race begins.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspiration is a hope or ambition.

clue.text: Moved in a worldly circle, perhaps

definitions.text: Moved in a worldly circle, perhaps

parts.words: Moved in a worldly circle, perhaps
parts.note: reads as mixing with high society, but a satellite moving in a circle around a world

explanation.surface: Someone who mixed in fashionable society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worldly circle' suggests sophisticated social sets; literally it is a path round a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel round a planet or star along a curved path is to circle it, as a moon does.

clue.text: Type of fish Tina cooked

parts.note: brill is a flatfish

indicators.note: cooked means altered, so the letters of the name are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tina cooks a certain kind of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type of fish' reads as one phrase, but 'Type' is the definition: brilliant is a very small printing type size. 'cooked' rearranges TINA to IANT.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing, brilliant is the name of a very small size of typeface.

clue.text: Loses script about a northern island

indicators.note: about means the script goes round the island

parts.note: MS is short for manuscript
Islay is an island in the Scottish Hebrides

explanation.surface: Someone misplaces a manuscript about a northern isle.
explanation.walkthrough: Islay is a Scottish island in the Inner Hebrides, famous for whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: To mislay something is to lose it by putting it somewhere forgotten.

clue.text: Military duds ?

parts.note: duds suggests failures, but is slang for clothes: soldiers' clothing

explanation.surface: A complaint about army flops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duds' is informal for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers wear standard regimental dress, the clothing all members wear alike.

clue.text: More than one bubble reputation for John Everett

definitions.text: More than one bubble reputation for John Everett

parts.words: More than one bubble reputation for John Everett
parts.note: John Everett is the Pre-Raphaelite painter famed for the picture called Bubbles; 'the bubble reputation' quotes Shakespeare's As You Like It

explanation.surface: A man's fame as fleeting as several bubbles.
explanation.walkthrough: His painting 'Bubbles', later used to advertise Pears soap, made his name, so his reputation rests on more than one bubble.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Everett, the Victorian painter, carried this surname.

clue.text: Fancy ring shown by artist

parts.note: to chime is to ring
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A decorative ring displayed by a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective describing the ring; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a fanciful, unreal idea or illusion.

clue.text: Note Thrale's love of the city

parts.note: C is a musical note
Hester was the wife of the brewer Henry Thrale, friend of Dr Johnson

explanation.surface: A letter mentioning Mrs Thrale's fondness for the city.
explanation.walkthrough: Hester Thrale, the diarist, was close friend of Samuel Johnson; Chester is a cathedral city in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester is a Roman walled city in Cheshire, England.

clue.text: No score before end of race — long-distance runner …

parts.note: nil is no score in a match

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Failing to score before the race finishes, a long-distance athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' suggests an athlete, but a river runs, and this is the longest in Africa. The dots run on into 22.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is said to run, and this one flows over four thousand miles.

clue.text: … may be depressed

definitions.meaning: following the dots from 21, the river may be the ... one, a tributary named by colour

explanation.surface: Continues the story of the runner: it may be feeling down.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join 21: the long-distance runner, the river, may be the BLUE NILE, which joins the White Nile at Khartoum.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low in spirits is called feeling this colour, and the Nile has a tributary of this name.

clue.text: Lucky thing being beheaded, of course !

indicators.note: beheaded means losing the head, the first letter

parts.note: a mascot is a lucky charm

explanation.surface: A good-luck charm loses its head — naturally!
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but 'course' is the racecourse in Berkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a famous racecourse near Windsor where Royal Ascot is held.

clue.text: Tell, a foreigner of high degree

definitions.meaning: to tell is to number off, as tellers do votes
a European nobleman ranking like an earl

explanation.surface: Inform on a highly ranked visitor from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell' suggests telling a story; it is the old sense of reckoning, as in 'all told'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to reckon a total and a continental nobleman equal in rank to an earl.

clue.text: No confused type of painter

parts.note: O, nought, stands for none
printer's pie is jumbled type

explanation.surface: Having no muddled kind of artist.
explanation.walkthrough: John Opie was an 18th-century Cornish portrait painter. Pie, also spelt pi, is printers' slang for type that has been spilled and mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: John Opie was a Cornish portrait painter and Royal Academician.

clue.text: Note for Cecil, keen collector of folk songs

definitions.text: Cecil, keen collector of folk songs
definitions.meaning: Cecil, the English folk-song collector of the early 1900s, also with keen meaning acute

explanation.surface: A message for Cecil, an enthusiastic gatherer of folk music.
explanation.walkthrough: Cecil Sharp collected thousands of English folk songs and dances; 'keen' also means the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a musical sign raising a note, and the surname of the folk-song collector Cecil, while also meaning keen.

clue.text: Ascribe to words of praise at first

indicators.note: first places the little word at the front of the charade

parts.note: a tribute is words of praise

explanation.surface: Give credit through words of praise, to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' reads as 'initially', but it tells you to put AT before TRIBUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: To attribute something to someone is to ascribe or credit it to them.

clue.text: So Turner and Yeats changed form of currency

indicators.note: changed signals the letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A painter and a poet swapped for banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner the painter and Yeats the poet; rearrange SO, TURNER and YEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasury notes were the paper money issued by the British Treasury during and after the First World War.
